Definition

  • Arrhythmia is disturbance in heart rate or rhythm
  • Arrhythmia can be congenital or acquired

Complications

  • Acute decrease in cardiac output => Heart failure
  • Degeneration into another arrhythmia such as VF
  • If continuous may lead to cardiomyopathy
  • Syncope or sudden death

Treatment

  • Medications
  • Transcatheter ablation
  • Pacemakers
  • Defibrillators
  • Benign PVCs is reassurance
  • Malignant PVCs are usually secondary to another medical problem
  • Treat the underlying cause
  • Lidocaine, amiodarone …
  • DC cardioversion
  • Anticoagulation before conversion
  • B blockers , CCB
  • Class I and III antiarrhythmics
  • Catheter ablation
  • DC cardioversion
  • Amiodarone, lidocaine, procainamide
  • Temporary or permanent pacemaker

Antiarrhythmic Drugs

  • Although majority of antiarrhythmic drugs are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in children; but most are still used off label
  • Arrhythmia mechanism may be different for the pediatric than the adult population.
  • There may be marked differences in antiarrhythmic drugs pharmacokinetics by age and in comparison, with adults.
  • Infants may have slower absorption and gastric emptying
  • Differing sizes of drug tissue compartments affecting the Vd
  • Hepatic metabolism and renal excretion may vary within the pediatric age-group as well as in comparison to adults
  • Antiarrhythmic drugs are categorized using the Vaughan-Williams classification
  • This system comprises 4 classes:
  • Class I includes agents that primarily block the sodium channel, This is further divided by the strength of the sodium channel blockade (a, b, c)
  • Class II drugs are the β-blockers
  • Class III includes agents that prolong repolarization by blocking potassium channels
  • Class IV drugs are the calcium channel blockers

Sinus arrhythmia

  • Normal physiologic variation in impulse discharges from the sinus node related to respirations
  • The heart rate slows during expiration and accelerates during inspiration
  • Occasionally, if the sinus rate becomes slow enough, an escape beat arises from the atrioventricular junction
  • Sinus arrhythmia characteristics
  • Variation in P-P interval
  • No change in P-wave morphology
  • No change in PR interval

Sinus bradycardia

  • Slow discharge of impulses from the sinus node,
  • Rate <90 in neonates and <60 in older children
  • Maybe associated with hypothyroidism, conditions with high vagal tone such as GIT obstruction or elevated intracranial pressure
  • Frequently associated with junctional escape beats and premature atrial contractions.
  • Sinus bradycardia characteristics:
  • P wave is present (sinus rhythm)
  • Rate is below 90 for neonates and 60 for infants and children

Wandering atrial pacemaker

  • Intermittent shift in the pacemaker of the heart from the sinus node to another part of the atrium.
  • It may also be seen in association with sinus bradycardia in which the shift in atrial focus is an escape phenomenon.
  • Wandering atrial pacemaker characteristics:
  • P wave is present but it differs in shape between beats (depending on its origin if it is sinus or atrial)
  • There maybe fusion between the sinus P and the ectopic atrial pacemaker

Extrasystole

  • Produced by the premature discharge of an ectopic focus that may be situated in the atrium, the AV junction, or the ventricle.
  • Divided into premature atrial contractions (PACs) and premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)
  • Isolated extrasystoles are of no clinical or prognostic significance, while frequent extrasystoles may be caused by organic heart disease (inflammation, ischemia, fibrosis) or drug toxicity.

PACs

  • Common in childhood, in the absence of cardiac disease.
  • Depending on the degree of prematurity of the beat and preceding R-R interval, PACs may result in a normal, a prolonged (aberrancy), or an absent (blocked PAC) QRS complex.
  • ECG shows either a premature P wave superimposed on and deforming the preceding T wave or a P wave that is premature and has a different contour from that of the other sinus P waves.
  • PACs may reset the sinus node pacemaker, leading to an incomplete compensatory pause

PVCs

  • Arise in any region of the ventricles.
  • Characterized by premature, widened, bizarre QRS complexes that are not preceded by a premature P wave.
  • Classified into uniform and multiform
  • Often, but not always, followed by a full compensatory pause.
  • Presence of fusion beats proves the ventricular origin of the premature beat.

Extrasystoles

  • Extrasystoles produce a smaller stroke and pulse volume than normal
  • Frequent, extrasystoles may lead to a definite rhythm, e.g., Bigeminy and trigeminy
  • Most patients are unaware of single PVCs, while some may be aware of a “skipped beat” over the precordium. This sensation is caused by the increased stroke volume of the normal beat +after a compensatory pause.
  • Anxiety, a febrile illness, or ingestion of various drugs or stimulants may exacerbate PVCs.

Criteria to furtherly investigate PVCs or not

  • ≥2 PVCs in a row
  • Multiform PVCs
  • Increased ventricular ectopic activity with exercise
  • R-on-T phenomenon
  • Extreme frequency of beats
  • Presence of underlying heart disease, a history of heart surgery, or both.

Tachycardias

  • Supraventricular
  • Ventricular

AVRT

  • Occur in presence of an accessory pathway
  • in conditions such as WPW syndrome

SVT Treatment

  • Vagal stimulation Valsalva maneuver, straining, breath holding, or standing on their head
  • Adenosine, DC

Refractory SVT

  • Holter monitoring
  • EPS studies

Atrial ectopic tachycardia

  • Tachycardia originating in a single focus in the atria

Multifocal atrial tachycardia

  • Originating from multiple different foci within the atria > 3
  • Common in infants without cardiac disease
  • Goal is to slow the ventricular rate

Accelerated junctional ectopic tachycardia (JET)

  • Automatic (non reentry) arrhythmia in which junctional rate > sinus node rate
  • Occur in early postoperative period after cardiac surgery
  • Reduction of infusion rate of catecholamines and control of fever and pain, amiodarone, sotalol

Atrial flutter

  • Supraventricular tachycardia
  • Intraatrial reentry circuit at a rate of 250-300 in children, 400-600 in neonates
  • AV node cannot transmit rapid impulses, so some AV block is always present

Atrial fibillation

  • Supraventricular tachycardia
  • Intraatrial reentry circuit that is more chaotic at a rate of 400-700 beats/min
  • Produces an irregularly irregular ventricular response and pulse

Ventricular tachycardia

  • at least 3 consecutive PVCs at >120 beats/min
  • paroxysmal or incessant
  • Associated with cardiac disease, prolonged QT interval, WPW syndrome and drug use

Ventricular fibrillation

  • Chaotic intra ventricular reentry rhythm that result in cardiac arrest
  • CPR and DC defibrillation
  • Amiodarone or lidocaine

Long QT syndromes

  • QTc interval > 480ms
  • Long QT is associated with torsades de pointes and VF => syncope and sudden death

Types

  • Mutations in cardiac potassium and sodium channels
  • 13 variants of long QT syndrome = LQT1, LQT2 …
  • LQT 1 induced by stress or exertion, LQT3 induced by sleep
  • Treated by B blockers , pacemaker due to bradycardia
  • ICD implantation

Short QT syndromes

  • Atrial or ventricular fibrillation
  • Associated with syncope and sudden death
  • Caused by a gain-of-function mutation in cardiac potassium channels

Sinus node dysfunction

  • Sinus arrest
  • Sinoatrial block
  • Sick sinus syndrome

Atrioventricular block

  • First degree
  • Second degree
  • Third degree
